newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: RTRS-INSTANT VIEW - Australian capex, wages data.
newsitem.headline: RTRS-INSTANT VIEW - Australian capex, wages data.

text.p: Australian private new capital expenditure fell 2.4 percent in the December quarter, the Australian Bureau of Statistics reported.
Median forecasts had centred on a 2.1 percent rise.

Equipment, plant and machinery expenditure rose 0.1 percent in the quarter while spending on building and structures fell 7.7 percent. The fifth estimate for 1996/97 investment came in at A$43.00 billion compared to a fourth estimate of A$42.910 billion and a fifth estimate in 1995/96 of A$38.104 billion.
The first estimate for expected capital expenditure in 1997/98 was A$34.68 billion, compared to a first estimate in 1996/97 of A$31,404 billion.
The bureau also announced that average weekly ordinary time earnings in the private sector rose 0.8 percent in the three months to November to be 2.8 percent higher over the year.
A selection of economists' immediate reactions to the data follows.
SAUL ESLAKE, CHIEF ECONOMIST, ANZ BANKING GROUP:

"What the AWOTE data suggest is a further moderation in the underlying pace of wages growth, which should be good news for the Reserve Bank and the financial markets. Although given the Reserve Bank's comments about activity in the bulletin and what Ian McFarlane has said, I doubt that this will raise the probability of another cut in official rates about 50 percent again...On the capex, the expectations data looks fairly encouraging for the next couple of years. The plant and equipment number does feed through into the national accounts, so we'll have a further modest increase in that after a pretty hefty 5.2 percent increase in the September quarter."
JOHN KYRIAKOPOULOS, SENIOR ECONOMIST, MACQUARIE BANK:

"I think the numbers we are seeing on the outlook for business investment are quite good. We're expecting double digit growth and that's consistent with the budget forecast which is for 17 percent growth. The cuts in interest rates in the second half 1996 are clearly working. We are looking for a good result in the the fourth quarter GDP. We think that consumption will be moderate reflecting the weak retail sales data, housing will make a positive contribution, but a number between 3.75 and 4.0 percent for year-on-year growth is what we will see."
HANS KUNNEN, CHIEF ECONOMIST, COLONIAL STATE BANK:

"We are still reasonably happy with the capex outcome. The bulk of it (the fall) was in buildings, and apparently most projects were put on the backburner. But plant and equipment rose 0.1, it remains at strong levels (and) is up 25 percent on the year and that is still driving the economy. The outlook for next year is reasonable. A 10 percent rise on the same time last year in terms of expectations shows a positive outlook. On the wages, private sector wages appear to be under control with structural changes giving apparent large wage rises to the public sector."
BRUCE FREELAND, CHIEF ECONOMIST, COMMONWEALTH BANK OF AUSTRALIA:

"I think the capex were a bit weaker than I was expecting, both in the quarter and for what it means for 1996/97, although certainly we're still expecting pretty strong growth in that year. The surprise to me was the strength of the expectations for 1997/98, looking at 10 percent up. That was a bit stronger than I was expecting and I think sets the scene for a continuing pretty good growth picture over next year as well. The wages data was in line pretty much with expectations and certainly showing the growth concentrated in public sector wages. A lot of that would seem to be due to compositional changes, so I would class it as more of a one-off rather than a continuing influence on wage
BRUCE HOCKMAN, SENIOR ECONOMIST, DEUTSCHE MORGAN GRENFELL:

"It validates the views of those who were looking for a strengthening in growth. There is a very strong momentum in capital expenditure expectations which is very important going forward, and it validates the sort of view the Reserve Bank was expressing that there is still a quite a strong recovery under way. And it looks like now that with the first readings of 1997/98 investment intentions that we can count on that capex continuing into the following financial year as well."
CHRIS CATON, CHIEF ECONOMIST, BANKERS TRUST:

"The December quarter capex was a bit weaker than we thought, but the weakness was in the very volatile and less reliable component, namely building. The plant and machinery bit feeds fairly directly into the national accounts and it was a bit weak in the December quarter and you may find people pulling back their GDP forecast by one tenth. The 1996/97 capex estimate expectations for a whole year remain robust and the first look at 1997/98 suggests that business at the moment expects the capital spendings strength to carry forward into 1997/98. The wages figures are roaringly good numbers. But it doesn't mean the Reserve Bank is going to say it will cut rates again."
GUY BRUTEN, ECONOMIST, SBC WARBURG:

"On the wages side, we were expecting a reasonably subdued picture on the private sector wages front anyway and this is slightly slower growth than we were expecting. But really, I don't think it changes the story too much. Private sector wages have decelerated quite a lot over the past 18 months or so. It's been an increase in public wages that really have been holding aggregate wages up. On the capex side, the quarter itself was a bit softer than we thought. Business investment will continue to be a driver of growth over the next two years."
ANNETTE BEACHER, SENIOR ECONOMIST, CITIBANK AUSTRALIA:

"The instant impression was that given the good wages (enterprise bargaining) data we got yesterday I think it helped to set the scene on wages so we were pleased to see such low figures. We are also noting strong data coming out of the public side, that has now happened for two quarters. But of course the better view is what is happening in the private (sector). It keeps all the pressures down, we are all looking for low inflation anyway, so it just basically confirms what we already know. It doesn't mean a change in policy at all.
